text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Sweden has some of the highest postage prices, making it cheaper to send a letter to Sweden than from Sweden, according to a newspaper survey of 14 countries. A letter can be sent anywhere from the United States for the equivalent of 2.5 crowns while in Sweden domestic stamps have risen to five crowns from 3.85 in one year.

- Interest for fuel produced from rape seed has risen strongly in the past year which will lead to increased demand for the crop. So far only OK and Statoil sell the diesel fuel which now accounts for half a percent of the diesel market.

- Liquidity among Sweden's listed companies is unusually high at the moment, rising 14 percent to about 190 billion crowns in 1996 and this rise continuing to over 200 billion crowns. Vehicle maker Volvo is at the top of the list with about 30 billion crowns in cash.

- Statistics show the percentage of drunk drivers who are women has risen to nine percent from four in the last two decades. But the number could be even higher: researcher Sonja Forward believes it is easier for women than for men to avoid law enforcers.

- Sweden is among those countries with the highest number of bankruptcies per capita. Despite a new law which came into effect last year to help save companies, only 200 companies applied for assistance compared to 10,610 bankruptcies.

- Pepsi will end its distribution agreement with Spendrups Bryggerier at the turn of the century and link up with rival Pripps Ringnes instead. Spendrups posted its best six-month results ever on Monday, showing a pre-tax profit of 35 million crowns, an improvement of 61 million crowns.

- People who invest in funds are the most heavily taxed shareholders in Sweden. A shareholders' interest group, Fondbolagens Forening, is asking the finance department to free small fund shareholders from wealth tax and apply the same tax rules across the board.

- Swedish truckmaker Scania said order intake in July for its best ever. The company posted a 36 percent fall in profit after financial items to 1.35 billion crowns in the first six months of 1997 but said the outlook was brighter. "We have now seen five months of an improved market and it is beginning to look more stable and certain," managing director Leif Ostling said.

- The half-year profit for Finnish telecoms giant Nokia Oy at 3.33 billion markka, up from 1.13 billion reported a year ago, was better than expected and the share rose on the result. A slower sales growth for its Mobile Phones division compared with the first quarter of 1997 probably stopped further gains in the share.
